title: The Saltmarsh Concord

cards.name: Veyra
cards.content: Veyra is the stilted city of the Saltmarsh delta, a hundred thousand people living one plank above the tide. It is divided into seven lanes of water that meet at the Round, the great plank plaza where the ferries dock. A single causeway runs from the Round to the Sea-gate. Visitors are told to follow the lamps, and to touch the wet plank of the landing stage before stepping onto the dry boards. The city has no wall; it holds that a person who cannot be refused cannot be an enemy. Its people are blunt, bookish and superstitious about water, and they greet each other with the words 'the plank holds'. The city's wealth comes from salt, paper and clockwork, and its politics from seven councillors who share one fragile gate.

cards.name: The Sea-gate
cards.content: The Sea-gate is a double leaf of oak and iron hung between two stone piers at the end of the causeway, a hundred paces across. It shuts the harbor mouth against storm surges and is the reason the city survives. The Sea-gate opens only when the Tide-clock strikes slack water, and it can be moved only by the windlass crews, who work it under the Tide Office's signal. The leaves are locked to the piers by seven iron keys that must all be turned together. Its seaward face is stripped grey by storms, and its great bell, rung at every opening and closing, can be heard across the whole delta. Tampering with the gate is punished by exile on the outer bars.

cards.name: The Tide Council
cards.content: The Tide Council is the seven-seat body that governs Veyra from the council hall above the Round. The seats are the Harbors, the Salt, the Brass, the Lamps, the Grain, the Letters and the Faith, and each controls one great power in the city. A law needs five votes. Opening or closing the Sea-gate needs all seven. The council meets in a long chamber with seven carved chairs and a floor of black marble inlaid with the tide tables, and its sessions are open to any citizen who has sworn the Plank Oath. In practice few attend, and fewer understand what they hear. The councillors are rich, careful and divided, and each holds a private grievance against the other six.

cards.name: The Tide Office
cards.content: The Tide Office is a tall brick tower beside the Round that houses the Tide-clock, the signal bells and the offices of the tide-wardens. From its top floor, a warden can see the whole harbor and the Sea-gate at the end of the causeway. The Office publishes the tide tables, which every Veyran trusts more than the weather, and it signals the opening and closing of the gate by bell and lantern. Its clerks are underpaid, overworked and fiercely proud, and they regard themselves as the keepers of the city's real clock. Visitors are not welcome above the second floor, and the stair to the tower is locked.

cards.name: Ledger Hall
cards.content: Ledger Hall is the grey brick headquarters of the Letters seat and the scriveners' guild, standing at the center of the Letters Lane. It holds the council's records, the guild's copying rooms and, beneath its cellar, the Salt Archive. The hall's great door is open from dawn to dusk to anyone with business, and its reading room is the quietest place in the city. Scriveners in grey move silently through its corridors carrying documents that nobody is allowed to read. The hall smells of ink, damp paper and pitch, and a visitor soon learns not to ask what a scrivener is copying.

cards.name: Brasswrights' Row
cards.content: Brasswrights' Row is the principal street of the Brass Lane, a clanging row of workshops where the city's instruments are made. The master of Brasswrights' Row is Mereth Quill, who has held the title for nineteen years and inherited her workshop from her teacher. The Row's guild makes the compasses, sextants and chronometers that Veyran ships carry across the sea, and it jealously guards its secrets. A visitor can smell hot oil from the Round, and hear the file and hammer before sunrise. The workshops are cramped, hot and full of half-built clockwork, and every apprentice has a story of a gear that took a year to cut.

cards.name: Gull's Landing
cards.content: Gull's Landing is a rotting stilt-dock on the edge of the Low Market, used by small boats and smugglers' cutters that do not want to be noticed. Gull's Landing is where Captain Brae docks the Gull, a long-hulled marsh cutter that is famous in the Low Market and notorious at the harbor office. The landing has a reputation for quick deals and long silences, and the reed-cloaked watch seldom ventures onto it after dark. The pilings are green with weed and the planks are slick with eel grease. A stranger who walks out on the landing without a purpose will find that every shutter along it has quietly closed.

cards.name: The Drowned Chapel
cards.content: The Drowned Chapel is the oldest sanctuary of Ossa in Veyra, a low stone building on the outer edge of the Round that sits half in the water. It was built on the oldest piles of the original reed island, and it is said that the Salt-Mothers swore the Plank Oath on its altar. The Drowned Chapel floods at every spring tide, and the priests have learned to live with wet floors and rusting hinges. A single brass lamp hangs above the altar and has never been allowed to go out. Visitors are admitted in silence, and offerings of salt and a small coin are left in a stone basin by the door.

cards.name: The Low Market
cards.content: The Low Market is the floating bazaar under the Round, a maze of rafts, awnings and rope-bridges where the poor of Veyra buy and sell. The Low Market is guarded by the Reed Watch, though the watch seldom goes far inside, and the market-mother keeps her own order. Stalls sell eels, rope, charms, stolen watches and fortunes told in tide-bones. The market never closes, and its smell, of smoke, tar and fish, clings to a visitor's clothes for days. It is the best place in Veyra to hear a rumor and the worst place to keep a secret.

cards.name: Lamp Quay
cards.content: Lamp Quay is the lamplighters' wharf, a long stone quay on the Lamps Lane where the lamp-bream catch is landed and the oil vats stand. It is also home to the largest counting-house on the delta, a dark stone building whose windows are always shuttered. The quay is lit by a double row of lamps that are never allowed to go out, and its tolls are collected by a guild of silent clerks. The oil smell hangs over the water, and the wharf is slick with fat. A stranger who loiters on the quay will be asked politely to move, and a second time less politely.

cards.name: Harbormaster Dov Haldane
cards.content: Dov Haldane is the harbormaster of Veyra, a stout, grey-eyed man in his late fifties who has held the post for twenty years. Harbormaster Dov Haldane answers to the Harbors seat of the Tide Council, and he is careful never to forget it. He wears a heavy signet ring and a coat of dull green, and he speaks slowly, as though every sentence were a contract he intended to honor. Haldane is not corrupt in the usual sense; he is simply a man who has never been in the room when a bribe was offered. He knows every captain on the harbor books and has a dry, patient kindness toward the young and the lost.

cards.name: Madam Orsolya Vane
cards.content: Madam Orsolya Vane is the keeper of the Salt Archive, a small, sharp woman in her sixties with ink-stained fingers and a voice like a closing door. Madam Orsolya Vane keeps the Salt Archive under Ledger Hall, and she has not left the building in a week in forty years. She is feared by clerks, trusted by councillors and respected by everyone who has ever tried to forge a page. Madam Vane has a prodigious memory, a dislike of untidy handwriting and a private conviction that the tides are lying to the engineers. She is polite to everyone and kind to almost nobody.

cards.name: Captain Brae Tolliver
cards.content: Captain Brae Tolliver is a smuggler of some renown, a lanky, sunburned man of forty with a gold tooth and a laugh that carries across water. Captain Brae Tolliver sells his cargoes to the Corvane Syndicate, and he spends the proceeds on rum and rope. He is charming, unreliable and surprisingly honest about his dishonesty. His cutter, the Gull, is faster than anything the harbor watch can field, and his charts of the marsh channels are worth more than the cutter. Brae has a short temper and a long memory, and he does not forgive being cheated, though he forgives almost everything else.

cards.name: Tide-warden Ketch
cards.content: Ketch is a tide-warden of the Tide Office, a thin, anxious man in his forties with a precise voice and a nervous habit of checking his watch. Tide-warden Ketch relies on brass instruments made in Brasswrights' Row, and he treats them with the reverence other men give to relics. He is the junior of three wardens who read the clock, and he is the one who actually does the work. Ketch is shy, honest and deeply loyal to the Office, and he suspects, with growing alarm, that someone is tampering with the readings. He does not know whom to tell.

cards.name: Brother Anselm Pike
cards.content: Brother Anselm Pike is an old priest of Ossa, a stooped, silent man in a patched grey habit with a face as wrinkled as dried reed. Brother Anselm Pike tends the Drowned Chapel, and he has done so for forty years without once leaving the Round. He speaks seldom and slowly, and when he does the words are usually about water. Anselm believes that the drowned god is waking, and that the city's pride in its gate is a mistake that will be paid for. He is kind to strangers, severe with the proud and absolutely incorruptible, which has made him a great many enemies.

cards.name: Mereth Quill
cards.content: Mereth Quill is the master brasswright of the Brass Lane, a broad-shouldered woman of fifty with a burn-scarred forearm and a laugh like a hammer on an anvil. She learned her craft from the old master and has surpassed him, and her workshop makes the finest chronometers on the coast. The Tide-clock is maintained by Mereth Quill of Brasswrights' Row, and she visits the tower weekly with a bag of oil and a file. She is blunt, generous and impatient, and she does not suffer fools or council visitors gladly. Mereth keeps a spare set of drawings for the clock in a hiding place that nobody knows.

cards.name: Councillor Ysolde Crane
cards.content: Ysolde Crane is the councillor of the Harbors seat, a tall, elegant woman in her fifties who dresses in dove grey and speaks in perfect, polished sentences. Councillor Ysolde Crane holds the Harbors seat of the Tide Council, and she holds it with a tact that has kept her in power through three scandals. She is cultured, cautious and a gifted listener, and her opponents say she has never lost an argument because she has never started one. Crane is privately terrified of the Corvane debt, and she has begun to wonder whether the Concord is worth the price of its survival.

cards.name: Lord Fenn Aldous and the Corvane Syndicate
cards.content: Lord Fenn Aldous is the envoy of the Corvane Syndicate, a pale, immaculate man of forty-five with a gentle voice and cold hands. The Corvane Syndicate is the offshore banking house that has been lending to the Salt seat for years. The Corvane Syndicate banks its coin in the counting-house on Lamp Quay, and Lord Fenn Aldous holds the mortgage on Gull's Landing, among a great many other debts. Fenn is polite, patient and always willing to wait. He believes in contracts as other men believe in gods, and he has been quietly collecting the obligations of half of Veyra for a decade.

cards.name: The Tide-clock
cards.content: The Tide-clock is a mechanism the size of a small house, standing in the Tide Office tower, that tracks the rise and fall of the sea. It drives a great dial visible from the Round and a signal that tells the windlass crews when to move the Sea-gate. It has run for a hundred and forty years and has never been wrong by more than a few minutes. Its gears are cut from brass in the Brass Lane, and its pendulum is a slab of oak weighted with lead. Tampering with it is a crime punishable by exile, and the tower stair is locked at night. Those who work beside it say that it hums when the tide turns.

cards.name: The Sea-gate Keys
cards.content: The Sea-gate keys are seven long iron keys of a pattern that no locksmith may copy, one for each seat of the council. All seven must be turned together to release a leaf of the gate from its piers. They are carried by seven sworn key-bearers who serve for life and may not marry into the great families. The keys are kept in a locked chest in the council hall between uses, and the chest has three locks of its own. A story says that when a key-bearer dies, his key is buried with him for a night and then recovered by the council, so that the dead may bless it. Nobody has confirmed the story, and nobody has dared deny it.

world_lore:
THE SALTMARSH CONCORD

Veyra is a city that was never meant to stand where it stands. It rises on tarred stilts out of the Saltmarsh delta, where nine slow rivers lose their names in a maze of reed beds, mud bars and brackish lagoons. From the sea it looks like a forest that has learned to carry lamps. From the inside it is a hundred thousand people living one plank above the water, trading, quarrelling and keeping accounts, and trying not to think about how much of the world beneath their feet is mud.

The delta is called the Saltmarsh because the sea comes into it twice a day. At high water the lagoons swell and the channels run inland for miles, carrying salt, fish and the smell of weed into the heart of the city. At low water the channels drain and the mud shows its ribs, and the people of Veyra walk the gangways above bars that were under a fathom of water at noon. Every child in the city learns the tide tables before learning to read, because a mistake on the mud has killed more people in Veyra than any war.

Veyra is built in seven districts, which the people call the Seven Lanes of Water. Each lane is a wide canal with a boardwalk on either side, and each is lined with the stilted houses, warehouses and workshops of one trade. The lanes meet at the Round, a broad plank plaza where the great ferries dock, and from the Round a single causeway runs out across the lagoon to the Sea-gate, the one place where the city touches the open sea. Travelers who arrive after dark are told to follow the lamps; the lamps on the lane posts are lit by hired lamplighters in a fixed order, and a visitor who learns the order always knows where he stands.

The weather of the delta is soft and damp for most of the year. Mist comes off the lagoons before dawn and lingers until the sun is well up, and in the cold months it freezes on the rigging and the rails until the whole city glitters. The wind blows from the sea more often than not, smelling of salt and tar. In late summer the storms come, and for three or four days the city shuts its shutters, ties down its boats and listens to the Sea-gate groan against the surge. Nobody in Veyra remembers a summer without at least one night when they were sure the sea would finally win.

Almost everything the city eats arrives by water. The marsh itself gives eel, mullet, reed hens and a bitter green called samphire, and the outer lagoons give oysters and a pale, oily fish the locals call lamp-bream because it is rendered for lamp oil. Grain comes down the nine rivers on flat barges from the farms upstream. Wine, olive oil, iron and cloth come in from across the sea. Veyra makes only a few things for itself: salt from the evaporation pans on the outer bars, brass and clockwork from the workshops of the Brass Lane, lamp oil, rope, tar and, above all, paper, which the Letters Lane sells to half the known world.

The people of Veyra are a mix of the marsh-born and the settlers who came after, and they are proud of the mix. The marsh-born are lean, quiet and superstitious, and they speak a low dialect full of tide words. The settlers came from the hill kingdoms and the sea-lanes, bringing guild habits and opinions on everything. Between them they have built a city that argues loudly and cooperates quietly. Veyrans say that a plank is only as strong as the weakest nail, and they say it so often that visitors assume it is a law.

A DRIFT THROUGH HISTORY

The city's own histories begin with the Salt-Mothers, seven widows who led a convoy of refugee fishing families into the delta after a plague emptied the coast. They found a reed island on a mud bar, drove the first piles into it with their own hands, and swore that no family would be turned away from the planks while the tide still came in. The oath, called the Plank Oath, is still sworn by every Veyran child at the age of seven, and it is the reason Veyra has never had a wall: the city holds that a person who cannot be refused cannot be an enemy.

For two centuries Veyra was a loose confederation of fishing villages on stilts, each with its own headman and its own gods. The villages quarrelled over channels and weirs, and their quarrels sometimes turned to knife work, but the sea was a greater danger than any neighbor, and they learned to keep a common watch. The great change came with the first salt works on the outer bars, which gave the villages something worth trading and, for the first time, something worth stealing. Within a generation the villages had stopped being villages and begun to be districts.

The year of the Great Surge is the hinge of the city's memory. A storm tide drove the sea three fathoms above its usual mark and swept away the outer lanes, drowning more than four thousand people in a single night. The survivors gathered on the highest planks of the Round and watched the water recede, and in the morning they met in the open air and made a decision that created the modern city. They agreed to pool the salt revenue, to build a gate that could shut the harbor mouth against the surge, and to govern the whole city through a council of seven seats, one for each lane. That agreement is called the Concord, and it gave the city its name.

Building the Sea-gate took thirty-one years. Engineers brought from three countries argued over the design for a decade, and the final plan, a double leaf of oak and iron hung from stone piers and worked by tide-driven windlasses, was drawn by a foreign woman whose name the city has deliberately forgotten, because it was she who warned the council that the gate would one day need a keeper it could not trust. The leaves were hung in the year the oldest of the Salt-Mothers' descendants died, and the city declared a holiday that has been celebrated every year since as Gate Day.

The two centuries since the Concord have been the city's golden age and its slow decline at once. The salt trade made Veyra rich, and the seven seats grew rich with it, and by the third generation the councillors were no longer elected from among the lane-masters but inherited, bought and bargained for like any other property. The Concord survived because it worked well enough that nobody wanted to be the person who broke it. The people grumbled, and paid their tolls, and told one another that the council at least kept the sea out.

THE TIDE COUNCIL AND ITS SEATS

Veyra is governed by the Tide Council, a body of seven councillors who sit in the council hall above the Round. Each councillor holds one of the seven seats of the Concord, and each seat has its own powers, its own revenues and its own long memory of grievances against the other six. The seats are the Harbors, the Salt, the Brass, the Lamps, the Grain, the Letters and the Faith. A law needs five of the seven to pass, and a motion to open or close the Sea-gate needs all seven, which is the closest thing the city has to a sacred rule.

The Harbors seat controls the quays, the ferries, the harbor dues and the watch that patrols the lanes. It is the most visible of the seats and the most hated, because every Veyran has stood on a quay at some point and watched a clerk count the copper he was about to lose. The holder of the Harbors seat appoints the harbormaster, who runs the quays day to day, and the harbormaster answers to the seat in everything but the oaths of his office. This arrangement keeps the harbormaster honest in theory and obedient in practice.

The Salt seat owns the evaporation pans on the outer bars and the royal monopoly on salt, which is the city's one great source of coin. It is the richest seat and the quietest; its holders seldom speak in council and almost never vote against the majority, because they have learned that a rich man who stays silent is more feared than one who shouts. The Brass seat represents the clockwork and instrument workshops of the Brass Lane and is the council's technical conscience. The Lamps seat controls the lamplighters, the oil monopoly and the bell-ringers who mark the hours, and it is the seat that most people know least about and depend on most.

The Grain seat feeds the city and knows it. The grain barges that come down the nine rivers must pass through the Grain seat's weighing sheds, and a bad harvest upstream is as much a political event in Veyra as a storm. The Letters seat runs the paper trade, the scriveners' guild and the great archive; it is the most literate and the most intrigue-minded of the seven. The Faith seat speaks for the old chapels and for the cult of the drowned god, and it is the only seat that is not purchasable, a distinction its holders guard with a fierceness that has sometimes saved the city and sometimes nearly ruined it.

LAW, THE WATCH AND THE PLANK OATH

Veyran law is short, and most of it is about water. A boat must carry a lamp after dusk. A gangway must be kept clear. A channel may not be blocked for longer than a tide. A person who finds a drowning stranger must throw a line before asking his name. These rules are enforced by the lane wardens, minor officials who walk the boardwalks with a staff and a ledger, and by the watch, which handles the things the wardens cannot. The watch is a force of reed-cloaked constables who patrol the lanes in pairs, and the people call them the Reed Watch because of the green capes they wear to be seen against the marsh at dusk.

Punishment in Veyra is mostly a matter of fines and labor. Thieves pay back three times what they took, in coin or in work on the gangways. Brawlers are sentenced to a season of mending nets for the harbor. The only crimes that carry exile are tampering with the Sea-gate and breaking the Plank Oath, and exile in Veyra means being rowed to the outer bars at low water and left there with a day's water and a lamp. The tide does what the courts do not need to. Most exiles who are lucky walk into the sea-road towns on the far shore, and are never seen again; the unlucky are found in the reeds a week later.

The Reed Watch is a small force, perhaps four hundred strong for a city of a hundred thousand, and it relies on the people to do half its work. Every household keeps a bell by its door and every lane keeps a rope of knotted lamps that can be pulled to raise the alarm. The watch is paid out of harbor dues, which is one reason the Harbors seat guards its control of it so jealously. The Reed Watch is commanded by Dov Haldane, the harbormaster, who inherited the post from his uncle and has kept it for twenty years by being competent, discreet and seldom in the same room as a decision that might embarrass the council.

The Plank Oath is more than a legend. Under the old law, any person who reaches the planks of Veyra and swears the oath may not be refused food, shelter or a berth on a ferry for the first three days. Corrupt landlords have found ways around the letter of the oath, and the Concord's lawyers have added a thicket of exceptions over the centuries, but the principle survives in every Veyran's conscience, and anyone who flagrantly breaks it risks being shunned by the whole district. A refused stranger is a story that grows in the telling, and the city's leaders have learned to avoid creating such stories.

THE LETTERS LANE AND THE ARCHIVE

The Letters Lane is the quietest of the seven lanes and the one with the longest memory. Its houses are built of brick rather than timber, a luxury that the Letters seat won by a dubious bargain a century ago, and its boardwalks are scrubbed every morning by apprentice scriveners who consider it an honor. Behind its tall, windowless frontages are the paper mills, the binderies, the ink sheds and the copying rooms where a thousand clerks produce the contracts, bills of lading and letters of credit that keep half the world's trade honest. A document stamped in the Letters Lane is accepted without question in ports that have never heard of Veyra.

At the heart of the Letters Lane stands Ledger Hall, a stern building of grey brick with a slate roof and a single great door. It houses the council's record offices, the scriveners' guild and the offices of the Letters seat. Beneath the hall, in a cellar cut down through the stilts and sealed against damp with pitch and lead, lies the Salt Archive. The Salt Archive holds every tide ledger written since the founding of Veyra, an unbroken record of the height and hour of every tide, for the city's engineers swear that no prediction of the sea is worth more than the memory of what it has already done.

The Salt Archive is guarded more closely than the council's treasury. Its single door is of iron, with three locks whose keys are held by three different officials, and its keeper is appointed for life. No ledger may leave the archive, and no reader may enter without a seal from the Letters seat. The reason for this severity is practical rather than sentimental: the tide ledgers are the foundation of the city's tables, and a forged page, silently slipped into the record, could mislead the engineers who set the opening of the Sea-gate. The archive has been robbed twice in its history, and both times the thief was a scrivener.

Scriveners in Veyra are a guild apart. They wear grey, they take an oath of discretion that is sworn on a blank page, and they are forbidden to discuss the content of any document they have copied. The oath is surprisingly effective; there are scandals in Veyra's history that have never been told because the only people who knew them were scriveners. A scrivener who breaks the oath is blinded, in theory, though no case has been recorded in living memory. In practice the guild enforces discretion by the threat of ruin: a scrivener who talks will never be hired in any lane again.

THE SALT TRADE

Salt is the source of Veyra's wealth, and the pans on the outer bars are the beating heart of the economy. The pans are shallow clay basins that fill with seawater at the spring tides and are sealed against the next flood. The sun and the wind do the work, and over a summer the water turns to brine and the brine to white crystals that are raked, dried and carried in baskets to the salt barns. Every basket is counted by the Salt seat's clerks, and every grain is recorded in a ledger that is sent to the Archive at the season's end. The city sells salt by the barge-load to the whole coast, and has done for six hundred years.

The salt monopoly is the Concord's fiscal foundation and its permanent temptation. The Salt seat holds the right to sell salt beyond the city, and it lets the other six seats draw a share of the profits in return for their support. Over the centuries the share has become a kind of dividend, and some councillors treat it as a private income rather than a public trust. Smugglers sell untaxed salt from the outer bars, and the harbor watch chases them with a determination that varies with the season and the identity of the buyer. Everyone knows that some of the smuggled salt ends up in the councillors' own kitchens.

THE BRASS LANE AND THE TIDE-CLOCK

The Brass Lane is noisy, hot and smells of oil and hot metal. Its workshops make the clockwork, compasses, sextants, chronometers and instruments that every sailor needs and every merchant buys, and they are famous across the coast for the precision of their work. The guild of brasswrights is jealous of its secrets, and a young apprentice may spend ten years learning to file a single gear before he is allowed to cut his own. The Brass seat holds the council's only real expertise in mechanical matters, and the councillors of the other seats consult it with a respect that they rarely show each other.

The greatest work of the Brass Lane is the Tide-clock, a mechanism the size of a small house that stands in the Tide Office tower and tracks the rise and fall of the sea in every one of its phases. The clock drives a great dial, visible across the Round, whose single hand sweeps from low water to high and back again. It also drives the signal that tells the Sea-gate's windlass crews when to move the leaves. The clock has run, with repairs, for a hundred and forty years, and in that time it has never been wrong by more than a few minutes. The people say that when the Tide-clock stops, the city will stop.

THE LAMPS AND THE LAMPLIGHTERS

The Lamps seat is the quietest power in Veyra. It controls the oil monopoly, the lamplighters, the bell-ringers and the signal fires on the outer bars, and through them it controls the rhythm of the city's day. The lamplighters are an old and secretive guild, descended from the first night-watchers of the reed villages, and they have their own customs and their own slang. They light the lane posts in a fixed order every evening, and a stranger who learns the order can navigate the city blind. Most lamplighters are marsh-born, and they treat the lamps as sacred.

Lamp oil in Veyra comes mostly from lamp-bream, a pale, fatty fish that is caught in the outer lagoons and rendered in great iron vats on the edge of the city. The rendering works are among the foulest places in Veyra, and the people who work in them are paid more than their trade deserves because nobody else will take the jobs. A smaller trade in imported oil exists for the wealthy, and the Lamps seat taxes it heavily. The oil monopoly is the Lamps seat's great weapon: a district that offends the Lamps seat can find its lane posts dark for a week.

THE DROWNED GOD

The old religion of the delta is the worship of Ossa, the drowned god, who is said to have been a fisherman swallowed by the tide who refused to die and instead became the tide itself. Ossa is neither kind nor cruel; he is the sea's indifference given a face. His chapels are low, damp buildings, often half-flooded, and his priests are lean, silent men who keep the lamps burning and the bells ringing. The cult of Ossa is the oldest institution in Veyra, older than the Concord and older than the city, and the Faith seat is its political voice.

Veyrans do not pray to Ossa in the usual sense. They make offerings of salt and a small coin cast into the water at the turn of the tide, and they say a short formula, 'Take the water, leave the plank', which is half a prayer and half a bargain. The priests teach that the sea gives and takes without malice, and that the only proper response to the sea is humility. This sits oddly with the Veyran pride in having built a gate against it, and the more thoughtful priests admit that the gate is an act of defiance that Ossa may or may not forgive.

THE SEA-GATE IN THE CITY'S LIFE

The Sea-gate is the only part of Veyra that the whole city agrees to fear. It sits at the end of the causeway, two stone piers a hundred paces apart with the double leaf of oak and iron hung between them, and on its seaward face the paint of a thousand storms has peeled in long grey strips. When the gate is closed the harbor is a lake and the city sleeps safe; when it is open the sea comes and goes as it pleases and the ferries run. The council debates its opening and closing in the most solemn terms, and the windlass crews who work it are treated as a kind of priesthood, exempt from the harbor tolls and fed from the council's table on feast days.

Tradition holds that the gate must never be opened or closed except by the unanimous vote of the seven seats, and for six generations the council has obeyed this rule. The rule has costs. In a bad winter, a single stubborn councillor can keep the harbor closed for days while the ferries idle and the salt barges queue in the lagoon, and merchants have been ruined by votes that took one hour too long. But the city accepts the cost, because the alternative, a gate that a majority could open against a minority's wishes, is a gate that could be opened by a bribe, and the council has never forgotten that the gate is also a lock on every household's door.

The gate's keys are the most closely guarded objects in the city. There are seven, one for each seat, and each is a long iron key of a pattern that no locksmith may copy. A leaf cannot be released from its piers without all seven turning together, which is the physical form of the unanimity rule. The keys are not carried by the councillors themselves, who might be bribed or threatened, but by seven sworn key-bearers who serve for life and are forbidden to marry into any of the great families. The system has held for two hundred years, and rumor says that it is only as strong as the weakest of those seven lives.

THE LOW MARKET AND THE LANES BELOW

Under the high boardwalks of the Round, at water level, lies the Low Market, a sprawl of floating stalls, mooring rafts and rickety platforms where the poorer people of Veyra buy and sell. It is the oldest market in the city and the only one open at all hours, because the stallholders live on their stalls and sleep under the awnings. The Low Market sells everything the high lanes do not: stolen goods, unlicensed medicine, fortunes told in tide-bones, eel pies that are not quite eel. The councillors profess to despise it and send their cooks there every morning for the freshest fish.

The Low Market has its own customs. Stallholders pay a small fee to the market-mother, an elected old woman who settles disputes and keeps a ledger of debts, and her word is binding in a way the council's is not. A thief caught in the market is judged by the stallholders in the open air, and the punishment is nearly always the same: he must work a week for the person he robbed. The Reed Watch patrols the edges of the market but seldom enters it, on the understanding that the market keeps its own order and the watch keeps its distance. The arrangement works because both sides pretend that it does not exist.

FERRIES, LAMPS AND THE ART OF ARRIVAL

The ferries of Veyra are flat-bottomed, lantern-hung boats poled by silent ferrymen, and they are the city's circulation. A ferry leaves the Round every quarter hour by day and every half hour by night, and a passenger who steps aboard pays a copper and is carried wherever the ferryman judges he wants to go. The night ferries carry a lantern at the prow, one at the stern and one on each thwart, and the arrangement of the lanterns tells experienced travelers which lane the ferry serves. A foreigner who boards the wrong ferry may find himself in the marsh before he realizes it.

Arrival in Veyra has its own ritual. A traveler who comes by water is expected to touch the wet plank of the Round's landing stage with his bare hand before stepping onto the dry boards, a gesture that is half greeting and half thanks to the tide. The ferrymen do not insist on the gesture, but they notice who makes it, and visitors who do tend to be offered a better price and a better berth. The ritual is older than the city, a survival of the reed villages, and the Concord's lawyers have never found a way to tax it.

THE OUTSIDE WORLD

Veyra trades with everyone and trusts nobody. To the north lie the hill kingdoms, whose barges bring grain, iron and timber down the nine rivers. To the east lies the coast road, along which a stream of caravans carries paper and brass inland. To the south lie the sea-lanes, and beyond them the Corvane Isles, a scatter of rocky islands whose bankers have made themselves the money-lenders of half the coast. The Corvane bankers have been circling Veyra for a century, offering loans that the city's seats find hard to refuse and harder to repay.

The relationship with the Corvane bankers is the most delicate in Veyra's foreign affairs. The Corvane houses lend against salt, and they have lent heavily to the Salt seat in bad years, and a debt of that size is a form of influence. The bankers are polite, patient and always willing to wait; they prefer to turn their loans into partnerships and their partnerships into obligations. Veyrans who despise them speak of the Corvane way as a slow drowning, and the phrase has become a kind of folk wisdom. Those who have worked with them describe the bankers as scrupulously honest in every clause and entirely ruthless in the sum.

THE MARSH AND ITS DANGERS

Beyond the last lamps of the outer lanes the marsh begins, and the marsh is not a place for the unwary. The reed beds hide channels that look like firm ground and mud bars that look like water, and the tide moves faster than a walking man across the flats. The marsh-born who guide travelers through it carry a long pole and a signal horn, and they navigate by the color of the reeds and the shape of the clouds. They say that the marsh remembers every person it has taken, and that on still nights you can hear them calling from the reeds, which the guides regard as a perfectly ordinary thing to say.

Smugglers use the marsh because the marsh protects them. A small cutter drawn by shallow-draft poling can slip through channels that the harbor watch's heavier boats cannot follow, and a cargo can be unloaded in the reeds and carried into the city on a hundred backs. The smuggling routes have names and histories; some are older than the Concord. The harbor watch knows most of them and watches a few, and the whole arrangement has the comfortable familiarity of a conflict that both sides would be sorry to see end. A smuggler who is caught pays a fine; a smuggler who is clever pays nothing at all.

FESTIVALS AND THE CALENDAR

Veyra reckons its years from the Concord, and its months from the moon. The calendar has twelve moons, named for the tides that dominate them: the Slack Moon, the Flood Moon, the Spring Moon and so on, and each has its own festival. The greatest is Gate Day, held on the first full moon after midsummer, when the Sea-gate is opened for a single hour at dawn so that the city may watch the sea enter its own house. The people line the causeway and the harbor wall, and the councillors walk the length of the causeway in their robes, and a child chosen by lot throws a handful of salt into the first wave. The salt is said to carry the city's thanks and its warning.

Another festival, quieter and older, is the Lamp Vigil, held on the longest night of the year. On that night every lamp in Veyra is put out at dusk, and the city sits in darkness for the space of an hour in memory of the drowned. At the end of the hour the lamplighters relight the lane posts one by one in the old order, and the city watches the light move along the lanes like a spreading wound closing. Visitors who experience the Vigil say that it is the one moment when Veyra, a city of merchants, seems entirely sincere.

CUSTOMS AND SAYINGS

The people of Veyra have a saying for everything. 'A dry boot is a rich man's luck' means that nobody in the city is ever entirely safe. 'The plank holds' is both a greeting and a blessing. 'He pays his tide' means that a person keeps his obligations, and 'she has gone with the ebb' means that someone has died or left without warning. Veyrans are suspicious of anyone who does not use these sayings, and a foreigner who learns a few quickly earns a small measure of trust, because it shows that he has listened.

Veyran hospitality is straightforward and slightly formal. A visitor who enters a house is offered salt and water before anything else, and refusing either is a minor insult. A meal is shared from a single dish, and the host serves the guest first. A bargain is sealed by touching the rim of a cup of water, not by a handshake, because water is the only witness the city fully trusts. Business is conducted slowly, with a great deal of apparent irrelevance, and a visitor who tries to hurry will find that the price rises with each hint of impatience.

THE GUILDS OF THE LANES

Beneath the council, the real texture of Veyran life is the guilds. Every trade has one, and every person in the city belongs to at least one, whether by birth, apprenticeship or marriage. The guilds set prices, train apprentices, settle disputes between members and, not incidentally, provide the votes that decide who sits in the council. A councillor who loses the support of his lane's guilds finds that his seat is suddenly a very uncomfortable place to sit, and the history of the Concord is largely a history of guild coalitions rising and falling around the same seven chairs.

The ferrymen's guild is the largest and the most closed. Ferrymen are marsh-born almost to a man, and the guild passes its poles from father to son as a kind of holy inheritance. A ferryman does not speak to passengers beyond naming the price, and does not remember their faces, and the guild treats a loose tongue as a kind of treason. The ferrymen know the tides better than anyone, and in a crisis the council has more than once relied on their silent judgment over the engineers' tables. A ferryman who says the water is wrong is almost always right.

The rope-makers, tar-boilers and caulkers form a loose federation known as the Low Guilds, whose members live in the cheapest districts and do the filthiest work. They are poor and proud and, in the memory of the older councillors, dangerous. Twice in the last century the Low Guilds have gone on strike, and twice the city has come within a day of running out of rope and pitch. Each time the council settled the strike by raising wages and quietly arresting the ringleaders, a policy that has produced a deep and enduring cynicism in the Low Guilds about the meaning of the Concord.

The Eel-wives are a guild of a different kind. They are the old women of the Low Market who catch, smoke and sell eels, and they run a network of information that rivals the council's own. An Eel-wife knows who has money, who owes it and who is about to lose it, and she is not shy about selling what she knows. Politicians and criminals alike court her, and a clever visitor to Veyra who wants a rumor confirmed will buy a smoked eel and ask the right question with a coin balanced on the counter.

THE HOUSES ON STILTS

A Veyran house is built on piles driven into the mud, with a boardwalk at the front and a landing stage at the back. The ground floor is a workshop or a shop; the upper floors are for living; the roof is a garden where the family dries fish, grows herbs and watches the lamps come on. Houses are built in rows, sharing party walls and pilings, so that a fire in one is a danger to ten. The lane wardens inspect the chimneys twice a year, and a household that fails the inspection is fined, and the fine is paid, because the alternative is a city on fire.

Furniture in Veyra is built to float. Every table, bed and chest is hollow or lined with cork, so that in a flood a family can sit on their own belongings and drift to the high planks. A well-made Veyran chair is a work of buoyancy engineering, and the best of them are sold for absurd prices to foreign collectors who have no idea that they are buying survival gear. Veyran children play at flooding games, learning to cling to cork-lined chests and call for a line, and the habits of catastrophe are woven into the city's playground.

THE MEDICINE OF THE DELTA

The physicians of Veyra are divided between the licensed doctors of the Letters Lane, who have studied abroad and charge accordingly, and the marsh-healers, who learned their art from their mothers and charge in fish. The licensed doctors treat the rich for the diseases of the rich, and the marsh-healers treat everyone else for the diseases of damp: fevers, lung rot, skin sores and the wasting sickness that comes when the mud gets into a cut. The two groups despise each other in public and consult each other in private, and a smart patient visits both.

The great killer of the delta is the marsh fever, a recurring sickness that comes with the late summer storms and lingers in the lower lanes for a month. It begins as a chill and ends as a delirium, and one in five of those who catch it die. The marsh-healers brew a bitter tea from reed root and willow bark that eases the fever, and the licensed doctors have never found anything better. Veyrans take the fever as a kind of tax, and the lanes that suffer most are the lanes that have the least say in council.

THE MARSH-BORN CLANS

Outside the city, in the reed villages that cling to the edge of the delta, live the marsh-born clans, the descendants of the original fishing families who never moved onto the planks of Veyra. They have their own dialect, their own gods and their own laws, and they regard the city as a rich, noisy and slightly dangerous cousin. The clans supply the city with eels, reed, fish and ferrymen, and in return the city supplies them with iron, salt and the occasional favor. Relations are warm on the surface and complicated underneath.

The clans are led by headwomen rather than headmen, a tradition that goes back to the Salt-Mothers. A headwoman is chosen for her judgment, not her birth, and her authority rests on her ability to resolve disputes without bloodshed. She is also the keeper of the clan's tide-lore, the accumulated wisdom of centuries of watching the water, and her pronouncements on the weather are treated with the seriousness that foreign courts give to royal decrees. The council has learned to consult the headwomen before any major engineering decision, though it rarely admits that it does.

THE SHIPS AND BOATS OF VEYRA

Veyra has never had a navy, and its merchants have never missed one. The city's safety rests on its shallow water and its gate, and what ships it owns are working vessels: deep-hulled traders for the long haul, flat-bottomed lighters for the lagoon, and the little poled cutters that the smugglers love. A cutter is thirty feet of pitch and planking with a lug sail and a single mast, light enough to be dragged across a mud bar and fast enough to outrun the watch. Every smuggling captain is a minor legend in the Low Market, and every cutter has a name that is a small joke.

The shipyards of the Salt Lane build the deep-hulled traders, which are the pride of Veyra's merchant fleet. A trader takes two years to build and twenty years to wear out, and the shipwrights treat each hull as a family heirloom. The yards are protected by an old custom: no shipwright may build a vessel for a foreign power without the Salt seat's permission. The custom has been bent a few times and never broken, and it is the reason that Veyra's rivals have never managed to copy its ships.

EDUCATION AND THE LITERARY HABIT

Veyra has an unusually high rate of literacy, and its people are proud of it. Every child of a lane-guild member is taught to read by the guild itself, and every child of the Low Guilds is taught by the chapel of Ossa, which keeps a school in every district. The curriculum is plain: letters, numbers, the tide tables and the Plank Oath. A child who finishes the chapel school is expected to be able to read a contract, check a bill of lading and recite the council's seven seats in order, and most can do all three before they are fourteen.

The city's literary habit shows up in everything. Shops advertise in verse, ferrymen swap proverbs, and the Low Market's street sellers have a repertoire of rhymes that they chant at the top of their lungs. The scriveners' guild publishes a weekly sheet of news and gossip, which is read aloud in every inn, and the better-off households subscribe to a dozen. A Veyran who cannot quote a line or two of local verse is regarded as slightly suspect, in the way that a foreigner who does not drink is suspect in a country of drinkers.

FUNERALS AND THE TIDE

Veyrans bury their dead at sea, or what passes for sea in the delta. A funeral procession goes by ferry to the outer bars at the turn of the tide, and the body, wrapped in sailcloth and weighted with salt, is lowered into the water as the ebb begins. The priests of Ossa speak the short formula, the mourners drop a coin, and the boat turns back before the ebb has carried the body out of sight. The belief is that the tide takes the dead to Ossa, who counts them and keeps them, and that a family whose dead are drowned well will never want for water.

The poor are buried in the marsh itself, in reed-lined shallow graves on the bars that the tide covers twice a day. The dead are said to rest more lightly there, rocked by the water, and the marsh-born regard sea burial as the only decent kind. Visitors who find the practice macabre are reminded that the alternative, a hole in dry ground, is a thing most Veyrans have never seen. For a people who live above water, the idea of being buried in earth is faintly absurd, and the idea of being buried in water is simply natural.

RUMORS OF THE SEA-GATE

In the last few years, the city has been full of rumors about the Sea-gate. The tides have been running strangely, some say, rising higher at the spring moons and falling lower at the neap, as though the sea itself were restless. The priests of Ossa say that the drowned god is stirring, and that the gate has begun to trouble him. The engineers say that the sea is only following the long cycles of the moon, and that anyone who sees a god in the tide table has been reading the wrong ledger. The Eel-wives say nothing, and sell a great many eels.

There are darker rumors too. It is whispered in the Low Market that the council is in debt to the Corvane bankers, that the debt is larger than the Salt seat will admit, and that the bankers have asked for something other than money in return. What they have asked for, the whisperers say, is the keys of the Sea-gate, or at least the right to hold them in trust. Nobody quite believes the whispers, and nobody quite dismisses them, and the councillors, when asked, change the subject with a smoothness that has convinced a great many people that the whispers are true.

A final rumor, perhaps the most dangerous, concerns the keys themselves. The seven key-bearers are old, and some are ill, and the rumor says that at least one of them has already been bought. The council, if it knows, has said nothing; the harbor watch, if it knows, has done nothing; and the Faith seat, if it knows, has retreated into the silence that its chapel guards so carefully. The city waits, in the way that it has always waited, for the tide to turn and show what the water has been hiding.

A WALK THROUGH THE SEVEN LANES

To understand Veyra, walk it. Start at the Round, where the ferries dock, and take the first lane to your left. Each of the seven lanes has a character as distinct as a province, and a visitor who crosses from one to the next in a single afternoon will feel as though he has passed through seven small countries joined by planks. The lanes are numbered in the old reckoning from the sea inward, but nobody uses the numbers; they are called by their trades, and a Veyran who tells you to meet him in the Grain Lane is not asking for a favor but giving you an address.

The Harbors Lane runs along the seaward edge of the Round and is the busiest of the seven. Its boardwalk is lined with chandlers, sail-lofts, ship's-biscuit bakeries and the offices of a hundred small shipping agents, and the air is full of the smell of tar and fresh rope. Gangs of porters trot along it all day with sacks on their shoulders, and the lane wardens stand at every corner with staffs held crosswise to keep the traffic moving. The lane's great landmark is the harbor office, a squat building of dark timber with a green door, where every captain who enters Veyra must declare his cargo and his name.

Behind the harbor office the lane narrows into a warren of ship-chandlers' yards, where old anchors hang from beams like rusted fruit and the owners sit on upturned barrels, smoking and arguing over the price of canvas. Children dart between the stacks of cable, and a pair of enormous grey cats patrol the length of the lane with the confidence of customs officials. The chandlers are notorious for their gossip; a captain who spends an hour haggling over a coil of rope will leave knowing which of his rivals is bankrupt and which has just taken a new mistress.

The Salt Lane lies to the east of the Round, along the edge of the lagoon where the salt barges tie up. It is the richest of the seven lanes by far, and it does not hide the fact. Its houses are three stories tall and painted in pale yellows and ochres, with carved balconies and shuttered windows, and its boardwalk is paved with real stone, which no other lane can afford. The salt merchants live here, and the shipwrights who build their traders, and the clerks who count their profits. A walk down the Salt Lane at dusk, with the lamps coming on one after another, is the closest a poor man ever comes to seeing what money looks like.

The salt barns of the Salt Lane are long, windowless buildings of grey timber, each as big as a cathedral, and each filled to the rafters with white heaps that glitter in the light from the loading doors. Clerks in aprons weigh and bag the salt, and every sack is stamped with the seal of the Salt seat before it leaves. The lane smells of brine and dust, and the dust is faintly sweet. In the busy season, when the barges come in from the outer bars, the whole lane is white with a fine drift, and the children are sent out to sweep it off the boardwalk in return for a coin.

The Brass Lane is the loudest place in Veyra, and its workshops start work before dawn. The sound of hammers and files, mingled with the hiss of the forges and the shouts of apprentices, can be heard across the lagoon on a still morning, and the people who live on the neighboring lanes have stopped noticing it, as one stops noticing the sound of one's own blood. The lane is narrow and hot, and its boardwalk is scorched in places where careless apprentices have dropped embers. Its houses are built of brick for fear of fire, which is a mark of the Brass seat's wealth and its caution.

The workshops of the Brass Lane are arranged in the old manner, with the master's bench near the window and the apprentices' benches in a row behind. A visitor who steps through the door is met by a wave of heat and the smell of hot oil, and finds himself in a room of astonishing neatness, every tool in its place and every drawer labeled. The brasswrights are proud of their order, and a master who allows a workshop to become untidy is regarded by his peers as a man who has lost his grip. Each workshop has its own trademark, a small mark stamped on every piece, and the marks are as well known across the coast as the crests of noble houses.

The Lamps Lane lies on the western side of the Round, a long, narrow street of low houses and dim doorways that is strangely quiet by day and strangely busy by night. Its inhabitants are lamplighters, oil-sellers and bell-ringers, and their working hours are the dusk and the dark, so that the lane sleeps through the morning and wakes up when the rest of the city is going to bed. A visitor who walks the Lamps Lane at noon will find shuttered windows and empty doorways, and may conclude that it is deserted. At sunset, a hundred doors open at once, and the lane fills with people carrying poles, ladders and cans of oil.

At the head of the Lamps Lane stands the Lamp House, a round stone building with a copper roof, where the guild keeps its records and its oil. It is a dark, close place, smelling of fish oil and hot metal, and its walls are lined with shelves of small brass lamps, each labeled with a name and a date. These are the guild's memorials: when a lamplighter dies, his lamp is retired to the Lamp House, and it is said that on the longest night of the year every one of them can be heard humming. The guildsmen deny this with perfect gravity, and nobody believes them.

The Grain Lane runs along the northern edge of the city, where the grain barges tie up. It is the most practical of the lanes, a straight, wide boardwalk lined with weighing sheds, storage lofts and the offices of the grain factors, and it smells of dust and damp sacking. The factors are shrewd, plain-spoken people who regard the other lanes as luxuries, and they take pride in being the ones who actually feed the city. A Grain Lane merchant will tell you without embarrassment that he could starve Veyra in a fortnight if he chose, and he will add, with equal sincerity, that he never would.

The Letters Lane, which we have already described, is the tallest and the quietest of the seven. It is also the most mysterious. The windowless frontages of its paper mills and copying rooms give nothing away, and the scriveners who walk its boardwalks in grey seldom speak to strangers. Rumors cling to it like damp. People say that the scriveners know the secrets of every family in Veyra, that they keep a hidden archive of scandals, that they can forge any signature on the coast. The scriveners say nothing, and their silence is the best advertisement the lane has.

The Faith Lane, the last of the seven, is the smallest and the oldest. It is a short street of low stone houses and half-flooded chapels on the southern edge of the Round, and it is the heart of the cult of Ossa. The houses of the priests are plain and cold, and the chapels are bare, and the whole lane has a stillness that is felt rather than heard. Visitors who enter the Faith Lane lower their voices without being asked, and the children who play there speak in whispers. At high tide the lowest steps of the chapels disappear under the water, and the priests walk about with their robes tucked up, perfectly unperturbed.

THE GREAT FAMILIES

Behind the guilds and the seats stand the great families, the dozen or so households that have held power in Veyra for generations. They are an odd lot, descended from salt barons, shipwrights, bankers and one long-forgotten admiral, and they intermarry with the careful ferocity of dynasties. Each has its own house on the Salt Lane, its own pew in the council hall and its own set of enemies. A Veyran child learns the names of the great families before learning the names of the seven seats, and can usually tell you which family currently dominates which seat, which is more than most councillors can do.

The Marrowgate family is the oldest, descended from one of the Salt-Mothers, and it has produced more councillors than any other. The Marrowgates are tall, pale and melancholy, and they carry their ancestry like a weight. Their house on the Salt Lane is a gaunt building of grey stone with a single tower, and it is said that the founder's chair still stands in the great hall, empty, waiting for the day when the Concord is restored to its original purity. The family has produced a dozen saints and a score of scoundrels, and nobody can quite say where one ends and the other begins.

The Dace family made its fortune in salt and keeps it in banks. The Daces are shrewd, round and genial, and they are the only great family that is genuinely popular with the Low Guilds, because they pay their debts and their servants on time. Their house is a comfortable, overstuffed mansion with a wide verandah and a kitchen that smells of baking, and its master, whoever he may be, is always to be found in the garden, in shirtsleeves, tending a row of marsh roses. The Daces are said to have no secrets, which is generally taken as a sign that they have the best ones.

The Rook family built ships, and the Rook yards on the Salt Lane have produced more deep-hulled traders than any other in Veyra. The Rooks are hearty, loud and impatient, and they treat their workers as family and their rivals as enemies. A Rook captain is a legend on every coast, and the family's blue-and-white pennant is recognized in ports from the hill kingdoms to the Corvane Isles. They have never held a council seat, which they regard as an insult, and the matter is a perpetual grievance at the family's long table.

THE LEGENDS OF OSSA

The stories of Ossa are the oldest stories in the delta, and every marsh-child knows them by heart. In the oldest version, Ossa was a fisherman who lived on a reed island before the city, a gentle man who sang to the fish as he caught them. One night a great storm tide swept the island away, and Ossa, clinging to a floating log, refused to let go of the world. The sea, which had never been refused, was astonished. It offered him a bargain: he could live forever, if he agreed to become the water. Ossa agreed, and the tide has had his face ever since.

A second legend tells of the three gifts Ossa gave to the first Salt-Mothers. To the eldest he gave a lamp that never goes out, and to the second a net that never tears, and to the third a word that the sea cannot refuse. The lamp became the Drowned Chapel's flame, and the net became the weirs of the marsh, but the word has been lost, and the priests say that every Veyran child is born with a syllable of it on the tongue. They add that if all the syllables were ever spoken together, the sea would stand still, and that this is why the Plank Oath is sworn by children.

A third legend, darker and less often told, concerns the gate. The story says that when the Sea-gate was built, Ossa came to the lawgivers in a dream and warned them that a wall against the sea is a wall against himself, and that he would not forget it. The lawgivers, who were practical people, ignored the warning, and built the gate anyway. Since then, the legend says, Ossa has been waiting, patient as water, for the day when the gate is opened by the wrong hands. The priests do not tell this story to children, and they do not tell it to councillors either.

THE BESTIARY OF THE MARSH

The marsh is home to a surprising range of creatures, most of them harmless and a few quite dangerous. The reed hen is a small, russet bird that nests in the tall grass and cries like a child at dusk, a sound that has frightened more visitors than any ghost. The mud-otter is a sleek, whiskered animal that hunts in the shallows and has a bad habit of stealing laundry. The glass-eel is a clear, almost invisible fish that is considered a delicacy and is caught by moonlight with fine nets. The marsh-born say that a glass-eel is the only honest creature in the delta, because it hides nothing.

More dangerous is the bog-lurker, a large, slow, olive-green reptile that lies half-submerged in the mud and snaps at anything that moves within reach. Its bite is not deadly but it is certainly painful, and the marsh-born carry long poles to prod suspicious logs. The tide-adder is a thin, banded snake that is active only at the turn of the tide and is as venomous as it is shy. Both are protected by an old custom, which holds that anyone who kills a marsh creature without need will be visited by bad luck, and the superstition is strong enough to keep even smugglers from shooting at them.

The night-herons deserve a mention. They are tall, grey, hunched birds that stand motionless in the shallows at dusk and are said to be the souls of drowned lamplighters. They have a habit of following boats, silent and pale, and a ferryman who is followed by a heron is considered to have a message to deliver. The herons are not hunted, and their feathers are never worn, and a Veyran who finds a dead one will put it in a reed boat and push it out to sea with a short prayer. Even the most skeptical engineers raise their hats to a heron on the water.

THE WEATHER AND THE SEASONS

Veyra has four seasons, though the delta is mild enough that the difference between them is chiefly a matter of light. Spring comes with the thaw in the hill kingdoms, when the nine rivers swell and the delta is flooded with brown water and drifting reeds. The air smells of mud and growth, and the first green shoots of samphire appear along the edges of the channels. The tides are high in spring and the Sea-gate is closed often, and the whole city is damp and cheerful and slightly dangerous, like a house in which a large party is about to begin.

Summer is long, warm and heavy with insects, and the marsh fever stalks the lower lanes. The salt pans on the outer bars fill with brine and the evaporation season begins, and the whole city smells faintly of salt and burnt sugar. In the evenings people sit on their rooftops and fan themselves, watching the lamps come on, and the older folk tell stories of the storms they have survived. The storms themselves come at the end of the season, a week or two of howling wind and driving rain that makes even the bravest sailor stay ashore.

Autumn is the most beautiful season in Veyra. The mist comes in thick and golden, the reeds turn the color of old brass, and the lamps burn with a warm, hazy glow. The grain harvest comes down the rivers on its barges, and the weighing sheds are full of laughter and dust. This is the time of the great fairs, when the Low Market spreads along every boardwalk in the city and the Eel-wives sell smoked eel at every corner. Winter, by contrast, is a gray, hushed season of fog and frost, when the canals freeze at the edges and the lamplighters carry hot bricks to warm their hands.

FOOD AND DRINK

The cooking of Veyra is built on eel, salt and onion. The classic dish is the eel pie, a thick, savory pastry filled with chunks of smoked eel, shallot and a splash of pale beer, baked in iron pans and sold hot from every corner stall. A good eel pie is a point of civic pride, and the arguments over the best recipe are among the longest-running feuds in the city. Other favorites include samphire fritters, lamp-bream grilled over reed fires, oysters served raw with vinegar, and a heavy dark loaf called tide-bread that keeps for weeks and tastes of molasses.

The Veyran drink is a pale, cloudy beer called marsh ale, brewed in the Grain Lane from barley, reed-honey and a secret herb that every brewer claims to have invented. It is served in thick clay mugs, slightly warm, and has a bitter, faintly smoky flavor that visitors either love or loathe on the first sip. Wine is imported from the south and sold at ruinous prices, and a visitor who orders it in a Low Market inn will be looked at with sad pity. The best drink in Veyra, according to the Eel-wives, is a cup of cold marsh water, because it tastes of nothing and reminds you where you are.

MONEY, WEIGHTS AND MEASURES

The coin of Veyra is the copper, the silver and the gold crown, and all three are stamped on one face with the Sea-gate and on the other with the seven chairs of the council. A silver is worth twelve coppers and a gold crown is worth twenty silver, and the exchange rates are fixed by the Salt seat and never altered. Merchants who travel abroad carry letters of credit from the Letters Lane, which are accepted in every port, and the city's reputation for sound money is its most valuable export. Counterfeiting is punished by exile, and a counterfeiter who is caught is sent to the outer bars with a purse of his own bad coin.

The measures of Veyra are as peculiar as its customs. Distance on the water is measured in poles, a pole being the length of a ferryman's pole, which is guaranteed by the guild to be exactly three fathoms. Weight is measured in baskets, a basket of salt being a hundred and eighty pounds, and volume in tides, a tide being the amount of water that a lagoon channel carries in an hour at the spring flood. Foreign merchants find the system impossible and the locals find it obvious, and the guild of weights and measures, a small, dusty body in the Letters Lane, spends most of its time translating between the two.

THE SEVEN SALT-MOTHERS

The Salt-Mothers are the city's saints and its founders, and the stories of their lives are told in every nursery. The eldest, Maren Holt, was a net-maker from the drowned coast, a stern, weather-beaten woman who had buried two husbands and a plague and feared nothing after that. It was Maren who first stood on the reed island and declared that it would bear a city, and her stubbornness gave the others courage. She is remembered in the city's oldest lullaby, which begins with the words, 'Maren drove the first pile deep', and ends, rather ominously, with the line, 'and the sea said nothing, for it was listening'.

The second Salt-Mother, Ilse Warran, was a midwife and herbalist, and it was she who taught the settlers which marsh plants could be eaten and which would kill them. Her book of simples, copied and recopied over the centuries, is still used by the marsh-healers, and a battered first copy is displayed in the Letters Lane under glass. The third, Tobbe Ansgar, was a boat-builder whose design for the flat-bottomed ferry is the same one used today; she is said to have laid the first keel with her own hands and wept when it floated. The fourth, Corra Vessel, was a trader who negotiated the first salt contracts and invented the letter of credit.

The fifth Salt-Mother, Hesper Lund, was a lamplighter, the first of the guild. She taught the settlers to hang a lamp at the end of every pier, so that boats lost in the mist could find their way home, and she walked the planks every evening, lighting the lamps herself until she died. Her lamp, a small, battered brass thing with a cracked chimney, still hangs in the Lamp House, and the guildsmen speak of it in lowered voices. The sixth, Wenna Tarn, was a judge, and drafted the Plank Oath in a single night. The seventh, Sibyl Orrin, was a priestess of Ossa, and it was she who made the covenant between the city and the drowned god.

Nothing certain is known of the Salt-Mothers' deaths. The chroniclers say that Maren Holt walked into the sea one evening and was not seen again, that Ilse Warran died in her sleep with a smile on her face and that Tobbe Ansgar was killed by a falling beam while launching her hundredth ferry. The others are said to have died in their beds, surrounded by their children, which is a more comfortable end than their city had any right to give them. All seven are buried at sea, and on the anniversary of the founding the whole city goes out to the outer bars in boats and drops a single flower into the water for each of them.

THE PLAGUE YEARS AND THE GREAT SURGE

Of all the catastrophes in Veyra's history, the plague years are the least discussed and the most deeply felt. A sickness came up the rivers from the hill kingdoms in the third generation after the Concord, a wasting fever that left its victims blue-lipped and cold, and in the space of two summers it killed one Veyran in three. The city shut its shutters, tied its boats and waited, and the Reed Watch patrolled the empty lanes with cloths over their faces, collecting the dead in flat boats and rowing them to the outer bars. The sickness ended as suddenly as it began, and left a silence that the city still carries.

The Great Surge, which came forty years after the plague, was a different sort of disaster, swift and violent and entirely natural. A storm tide drove the sea three fathoms above its usual mark and swept away the outer lanes in a single night, drowning four thousand people. The survivors, huddled on the highest planks of the Round, watched the dawn come up over a ruined city and made the decision that created the Concord. The memory of the Surge is the reason Veyrans are so careful about the gate, and so intolerant of anyone who treats it carelessly. The marks of the flood are still visible on the pilings of the Round, a line of green slime two fathoms above the present tide.

THE CORVANE WARS

The wars between Veyra and the Corvane Isles are a strange chapter in the city's history, because they were fought almost entirely with paper. The Corvane bankers, seeing the value of Veyra's salt, attempted to buy the monopoly outright, and the Salt seat, outraged, refused. The bankers responded by calling in a series of loans, and a financial war began that lasted eleven years and ruined a dozen families on both sides. The Salt seat survived by selling its reserves of grain, and the bankers withdrew, humiliated but not defeated, to nurse their grievance and plan a more patient return.

The Corvane bankers have never forgotten the failure. Their families tell the story to their children as a lesson in the limits of force, and the lesson they draw is that the way to take a city is not to attack it but to lend to it. They have been lending to Veyra for a century, in small amounts, in small ways, and the debts have accumulated with the quiet inevitability of silt. A Corvane banker will tell you, with a smile, that he is not an enemy of the city but its oldest friend, and he will mean it, in the way that a tide is a friend to a harbor.

THE REED STRIKE

The Reed Strike, which took place a century ago, is the great episode of the Low Guilds' history. The rope-makers, caulkers and tar-boilers, tired of low wages and high tolls, laid down their tools in a single night and refused to work. Within a week the ferries had stopped, the lamps had gone out in the poorer lanes and the city was choking on its own refuse. The council, which had been ignoring the Low Guilds for decades, found itself facing the one thing it could not buy off: a general strike that threatened the safety of the gate. The strike lasted nineteen days and ended with a compromise that satisfied nobody.

The leader of the strike was a woman named Berta Quill, a caulker's daughter with a voice that could carry across a canal. She spoke at every meeting, in every lane, in the plain, ringing language of the marsh, and by the end of the first week she had half the city on her side. When the council finally agreed to negotiate, it demanded her arrest as a precondition, and she walked into the council hall of her own accord, with her chin up and her hands unbound. She was sentenced to a year on the outer bars, which in Veyra is a death sentence, and the whole city came out to watch her go. She is said to have walked back on the next low tide, with her hair full of salt, and nobody dared arrest her again.

THE OUTER BARS

Beyond the harbor mouth, a chain of low sandbars stretches out into the sea, and these are the outer bars, the place where the salt is made and where the exiles are left. The bars are flat, windswept and almost entirely without shelter, and at high water the sea washes over them to a depth of a hand or two. The salt-workers live on stilted huts at the edge of the pans, tough, sunburned people who speak a dialect of their own and are fiercely proud of their trade. They tell strangers that the bars are the true heart of Veyra, and that the city is merely their warehouse.

The pans themselves are an extraordinary sight, a geometric pattern of shallow clay basins stretching for miles, some silvery with water, some blinding white with crystal. The salt-workers move across them on boards, raking the crust into heaps, and from a distance they look like ants on a chessboard. The work is hard and monotonous, and the glare gives the workers a permanent squint, but the pay is good and the community is close. They have their own festival, the Raking, held at the end of the season, when the whole population gathers on the biggest pan and dances barefoot on the salt.

THE REED VILLAGES

The reed villages of the marsh-born are clusters of low, thatched houses built on artificial islands of woven reed and mud, each linked to its neighbors by a web of causeways and canoe-paths. A village may have a hundred inhabitants or a thousand, and each has its own headwoman, its own boat-yard and its own weaving tradition. The houses are low and round, with conical thatched roofs, and they rock slightly in the wind, so that a visitor who sleeps in one for the first time often wakes believing that he is at sea. The marsh-born regard this as perfectly normal and wonder how anyone sleeps on solid ground.

The marsh-born are generous hosts and difficult friends. A traveler who arrives at a village is given food and a bed without a question, but the second day he is expected to work, and the third day he is expected to have an opinion about the tides. The villagers are blunt, funny and entirely unsentimental, and they find the city dwellers' habit of lying politely incomprehensible. Their law is simple and strictly enforced: a person who harms the marsh, or a neighbor, or a guest, is banished to the outer bars. The punishment is rare, and it is not remembered kindly.

PAPER, INK AND THE ART OF THE SCRIVENER

The paper of Veyra is the finest on the coast, and its making is a secret guarded by the Letters seat. The mills on the Letters Lane use rags from the hill kingdoms, marsh reed and a pale clay from the outer bars, and the proportions are known only to the master-papermakers. A sheet of Veyran paper is thin, strong, nearly white and almost impervious to damp, which is the quality that made the city's name. Contracts, deeds and letters of credit written on it are accepted as proof in half the courts of the world, and the city has done nothing to discourage the belief that the paper itself is a kind of truth.

Veyran ink is made from oak galls, iron salts and a black pigment extracted from lamp-bream oil, and it is indelible. A document written in Veyran ink cannot be scraped, washed or burned clean without leaving a ghost of itself on the paper, and the scriveners' guild has built a quiet industry out of detecting forgeries. A trained scrivener can tell, by the shade of an ink and the angle of a stroke, whether a page was written in a hurry or a rage or a lie. The best of them are consulted by courts, banks and councils, and they charge accordingly.

THE ART OF CLOCKWORK

The clockwork of the Brass Lane is the most delicate craft in the city. A master brasswright will cut a gear no wider than a thumbnail, with teeth so fine that they cannot be seen without a lens, and set it in a movement that will run for a century without losing a minute. The secret, the brasswrights say, is not in the cutting but in the listening: a master can hear a fault in a mechanism as a musician hears a flat note, and will stop a whole workshop to chase a tick that nobody else can detect. The best brasswrights never speak while they work, and the Row is quietest at the hours when it is busiest.

The oil of the Brass Lane is as precious as its metal. The brasswrights use a fine, pale oil pressed from the livers of deep-sea fish, which does not gum or freeze or turn rancid, and they buy it at ruinous prices from a single dealer on Lamp Quay. The oil is stored in small lead flasks in cool cellars, and a workshop that runs out of it is considered to be in disgrace. Apprentices learn to apply it with a single drop on the tip of a feather, and a drop too many is punished by a day spent cleaning forges.

LAW CASES AND FAMOUS TRIALS

Veyran lawyers are fond of precedent, and the city's courts are full of famous trials that are cited and re-cited with the relish of a theologian quoting scripture. The Case of the Floating Chair, for instance, settled the question of whether a cork-lined chair that drifts into a neighbor's house is salvage or theft, and the answer, which depends on the color of the chair, is still debated.
