The Case of the Dry Boot established that a person who steps onto another's dock without invitation is liable for any damage done by the tide. The Case of the Three Lamps, which concerned a lamplighter accused of lighting a lamp too early, ran for eleven years and ended in an acquittal and a riot.

The most famous trial of all is the Trial of the Salt Clerk, in which a junior clerk of the Salt seat was accused of stealing a basket of salt and defended himself by arguing that salt, being a gift of the sea, belonged to no one. The judges, who were all salt merchants, were so appalled that they sentenced him to the outer bars, and the clerk, a sturdy and philosophical young man, walked out across the mud and returned a week later with a basket of salt on his shoulder. He placed it on the judges' table and said, politely, that he had been right. The judges, after a long silence, adjourned for lunch, and the clerk was never prosecuted again.

PROVERBS AND SMALL SUPERSTITIONS

Veyrans are superstitious in small, practical ways. It is bad luck to whistle on a boat, to step on a gangway with the left foot first, to name the sea after dark or to count the lamps on a post. It is good luck to be spat on by a ferryman, to find a coin in a fish and to hear a night-heron cry on your left hand. A baby is never carried across a bridge on the day of its naming, and a bride never wears a pin in her hair. These customs are not taken very seriously, but they are rarely broken, and a stranger who breaks one will be told, politely, to knock on the nearest piling.

Every trade has its own set of sayings, and the Veyrans love to quote them. The ferrymen say, 'The pole knows the bottom.' The brasswrights say, 'A fault is a promise broken.' The lamplighters say, 'Light the next one first.' The scriveners say nothing, which is itself a kind of saying. The Eel-wives say, 'An honest eel is a dead eel,' and the priests say, 'The tide is not a judge, but it keeps the books.' A Veyran who wants to end an argument will quote the nearest proverb, and the other party is obliged to quote a better one or concede.

THE ROUND AND THE COUNCIL HALL

The Round, the great plank plaza at the heart of the city, is the largest open space in Veyra and the only place where the whole population can gather at once. It is a perfect circle, three hundred paces across, made of oak planks laid in a spiral pattern over a forest of piles, and its surface is worn smooth and dark by six centuries of feet. At the center stands a small stone pillar, the Zero Post, from which all distances in the city are measured. The council hall stands on the north side of the Round, a stern white building with seven tall windows, one for each seat, and the Tide Office tower rises on the east.

The council hall is a handsome, severe building. Its long chamber has a black marble floor inlaid with the tide tables of the first century, and the seven carved chairs stand on a low dais at one end. The walls are hung with the portraits of past councillors, whose painted eyes follow the visitor with an expression of grave disapproval. The acoustics of the room are extraordinary: a whisper at one end can be heard at the other, and the councillors have learned, over generations, to speak softly in it. The great doors are carved with scenes from the founding, and the central panel shows the Salt-Mothers driving the first pile into the mud.

THE TIDE TABLES AND THE ART OF PREDICTION

The tide tables of Veyra are the oldest continuous scientific record on the coast. Every tide for six centuries has been measured, written down and filed, and the engineers of the Tide Office use the accumulated record to predict the height and hour of every future tide with remarkable accuracy. The method is simple in principle and tedious in practice: the engineers compare each tide to the tides of the same moon in previous years, correct for the wind and the weather, and publish a figure that is rarely wrong by more than an inch. The tables are published annually and are bought by every ship's captain on the coast.

The engineers of the Tide Office are quietly convinced that the tides have a pattern that no one has yet understood. They speak, in their private moments, of long cycles of nineteen years and of subtle shifts in the moon's orbit, and they have filled a dozen notebooks with calculations that nobody outside the Office has seen. The priests of Ossa regard this as hubris, and the engineers regard the priests as superstitious, and the two groups maintain an uneasy truce, based on the shared recognition that the sea does not care what either of them believes.
